summary: Cedric Vidal opens by contrasting his topic with the preceding red teaming session: while red teaming generates adversarial data to test AI in bad situations, this talk covers traditional dataset-based evaluation of AI agents. He stresses that as agents gain autonomy, the risk of creating havoc increases, making systematic evaluation essential. He argues evaluation should start at the very beginning of an AI project, not after the app is built. He outlines four layers of protection: model and safety system (platform-level, built into Azure), system message and grounding, user experience, and application-layer mitigations. The foundational model is just one part; real safety comes from layering smart mitigations at the application layer. Vidal demonstrates manual model evaluation using the VS Code AI Toolkit plugin, comparing GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.0 side by side on a panna cotta recipe prompt, noting 4.1's major throughput improvement and preferred answer quality. He then builds an AI agent that extracts event information from web pages using the Playwright MCP server, customizing an auto-generated agent template. He shows batch evaluation on a small dataset within VS Code, including a case where the agent navigated from a Reactor event page to a linked Luma page to find attendee counts. To scale beyond manual eyeballing, Vidal introduces Azure Foundry's built-in evaluators: AI-assisted quality checks (groundedness, fluency, coherence), classic NLP metrics (F1, BLEU, ROUGE), and AI-assisted risk and safety evaluators. He then shows evaluation results on a camping-themed dataset, demonstrating configurable thresholds on a 1-5 scale, with different thresholds appropriate for different industries (gaming vs kids apps). Vidal also demonstrates multimodal evaluation mixing text and images, showing a violent image that scored 4 out of 5 on safety—not the maximum 5, thus failing by default, but adjustable for contexts like violent video games. He closes by sharing resources: Azure Foundry GitHub discussions, Discord server, and his contact information, noting slides will be posted to Discord.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Evaluation should begin at project inception, not after the application is built

Azure Foundry evaluators support configurable thresholds (1-5 scale) tailored to application context, e.g., gaming vs children's apps
Multimodal evaluation supports mixing text and images, including multi-turn conversations

Agents can autonomously navigate across linked web pages to gather information not present on the original source page

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.summary: Cedric Vidal introduces himself and distinguishes his topic from the preceding red teaming session, focusing on traditional dataset-based evaluation. He notes the increasing risk as agents gain autonomy.

sections.title: Four Layers of Protection and When to Evaluate
sections.summary: Vidal explains evaluation should start at project inception. He outlines four layers: model/safety system (Azure built-in), system message/grounding, user experience, and application-layer mitigations. The model is just one part; real safety comes from layered application mitigations.

sections.title: Manual Model Evaluation Demo (VS Code AI Toolkit)
sections.summary: Demonstrates side-by-side comparison of GPT-4.1 vs GPT-4.0 on a panna cotta recipe prompt using the VS Code AI Toolkit plugin, noting 4.1's superior throughput and answer quality.

sections.title: Building and Customizing an AI Agent
sections.summary: Shows building a web exploration agent using Playwright MCP server in AI Toolkit, customizing it to extract event name, date, location, and attendee count from a Luma event page. The agent autonomously navigated to a linked Luma page to find attendee counts.

sections.title: Batch Evaluation and Code Generation
sections.summary: Demonstrates running the agent on a small dataset within VS Code, manually marking thumbs up/down, exporting results to JSON line files, and generating boilerplate code for frameworks like OpenAI Agents.

sections.title: Scaling with Azure Foundry Evaluators
sections.summary: Introduces Azure Foundry's built-in evaluators: AI-assisted quality checks (groundedness, fluency, coherence), NLP metrics (F1, BLEU, ROUGE), and risk/safety evaluators. Shows a Python notebook for programmatic evaluation via Azure AI Foundry, not executed due to time.

sections.title: Evaluation Results, Thresholds, and Multimodal Demo
sections.summary: Shows evaluation results on a camping-themed dataset with configurable 1-5 score thresholds, explaining different thresholds suit different industries (gaming vs kids apps). Demonstrates multimodal evaluation mixing text and images, including a violent image that scored 4 out of 5—failing by default but adjustable for contexts like video games. Closes with resources: Azure Foundry GitHub discussions, Discord server, and contact info. Slides to be shared on Discord.
